speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: that Bill C-112, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act, the Access to Information Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Customs Act, the Federal Court Act, the Income Tax Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act, the Tax Rebate Discounting Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and a related Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak on second reading of Bill C-112.
This bill contains amendments that were proposed in the notice of Ways and Means motion tabled on December 9, 1992. It contains refinements to the goods and services tax that have been developed through extensive consultations with businesses, organizations, tax professionals and individuals during the first two years that the tax has been in place. These measures reinforce the government's commitment to the smooth and efficient operation of the GST.
With a major tax reform such as the replacement of the federal sales tax with the GST inevitably refinements must be made to the system as the government and the private sector together draw on the practical experience of seeing the tax at work in the marketplace.
The proposed amendments are technical in nature. As such, they do not substantially alter the way in which the GST operates. But this does not diminish the importance
of this legislation, for these measures represent a rigorous fine tuning of the details of the tax. They simplify GST compliance across many sectors of the economy.
Over the past two years since the GST was implemented we have actively consulted industry associations, organizations and businesses, large and small. We responded to their suggestions with concrete proposals on how to improve the operation of the tax in specific industries.
Allow me to mention just a few examples of the changes that are contained in this bill. Following consultations with the Canadian taxi-cab industry the government proposed adjustments to the operation of the GST in this industry so that it could use a consistent pricing structure.
We heard representations from direct selling organizations whose sales contractors sell household goods door to door. As a result of these discussions we are proposing new rules under which hundreds of thousands of independent sales contractors do not have to register and file GST returns.
For retailers the bill contains amendments that would simplify the operation of the tax for a wide variety of special types of transactions, ranging from the treatment of discount coupons to the treatment of returnable beverage containers. In addition, simplified rules have been designed specifically for situations where retailers make purchases through buying groups. These special rules would significantly reduce the amount of paperwork that would otherwise be required under the normal rules of the tax. These changes have also been supported by associations representing manufacturers and distributors of grocery products.
We also introduced changes simplifying the operation of the tax in areas where activities are often undertaken by joint ventures. These proposals have been supported by the oil and gas industry.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
The improvements to the tax system that are reflected in this bill will make Canadian industry more efficient and competitive, both in foreign and domestic markets. For example, there is a proposal that would improve the competitive position of service exporters by allowing them to import goods for servicing without having to pay tax on the importation.
In addition, the bill provides broader relief under the tourist and foreign convention rebate program, a program that is already unequalled among other countries that have similar tax systems. This would enhance the competitiveness of our tourism and convention industry by helping to maintain the attractiveness of Canada as a destination for foreign visitors.
These are not the only measures that would strengthen the international competitiveness of Canadian suppliers. We received representations from businesses requesting changes to the GST to facilitate the export of goods and services by these companies to their foreign customers. In response to these representations this bill proposes refinements that will be particularly welcomed by auto parts manufacturers in southern Ontario centres such as Windsor and Oshawa.
The Bill also contains proposals that would directly benefit consumers in need. These include additions to the list of tax-free medical devices and prescription drugs.
Finally, the government is also proposing a special credit for certified institutions that employ mentally or physically disabled individuals. This credit was designed in recognition of the unusually high costs faced by these institutions during the transition to the GST.
This bill contains proposals to allow Canadians who live year-round in travel trailers to rent their trailer sites on a tax-exempt basis, thereby providing them with the same treatment as other residential tenants. In addition, this bill provides a simpler and more generous GST housing rebate to individuals who build their own homes.
The measures included in this bill improve upon the operation of the GST in the retail, farming, oil and gas, export and tourism sectors, to name but a few.
This bill makes the tax fairer for tenants and homeowners alike, and helps consumers in need. All of these
stand to benefit in one way or another from specific amendments contained in this bill.
An important objective of the government is to simplify compliance with the tax system, especially for small businesses. To this end the bill contains measures that would allow for greater flexibility with respect to reporting requirements. These measures include a plan that would make it easier for up to one million businesses to file GST returns only once a year.
The Bill would make the GST not only simpler but fairer for businesses. It gives the Minister of National Revenue discretion to waive penalties and interest in cases where someone is unable to file a return or make a remittance on time due to extraordinary circumstances beyond his or her control.
When this legislation was in draft form it was studied by tax experts. It is indeed noteworthy that they applauded the many streamlining improvements and clarifications contained in it. They have also urged speedy passage of the legislation in order to reduce uncertainty in the application of the tax.
In closing, I would like to emphasize that this bill is the result of extensive consultations with businesses, organizations, individual Canadians and their professional advisors. We have worked together to identify specific problems in particular areas of the GST and today we are proposing workable solutions that are tailored to the realities of today's marketplace.
This bill reflects representations made by members of all major parties on behalf of their constituents. It corrects anomalies and clarifies the application of the tax laws. Therefore I urge hon. members to give their full support to this bill and to ensure that it is approved as soon as possible, because these adjustments will make life easier for many people.

Madam Speaker, I listened to the hon. member on the government side while he was giving his speech and I heard the words: a simpler GST, a fairer GST and the fact that the government was working together with business in refining the GST.
March 12, 1993

Here we are almost three years later with 350 pages of simplification. This whole GST operation by the government has been the worst initiative that any government has ever perpetrated on a people.
Today people want their politicians to focus on one issue: putting people back to work. That is the priority issue. Whenever an initiative or a bill has come before this House that would help in any way, shape or form to put people back to work we on this side of the House have co-operated.
Madam Speaker, two weeks ago you were sitting in the chair when we debated the Small Businesses Loans Act. It was a Friday, it was third reading, but I can remember we also sat on the previous Tuesday. We worked with the government uninterrupted for 10 hours to make sure the Small Businesses Loans Act was put through this House in record breaking time so that it would be an instrument to assist the small business community, the 960,000 businesses whose sales are under $5 million. We, the Liberal Party of Canada, co-operated with the government. We applauded the government for this initiative. Small businesses can go to their local financial institutions or credit unions and get a Government of Canada loan guarantee of up to $250,000.
When government members from time to time hurl insults across this way suggesting that we are not working with them, that we are not constructive, they cannot say that we did not co-operate on that specific bill, a bill that could put people back to work immediately if properly utilized.
I have observed two things since that bill was passed. First, the government made a commitment that it was going to promote the bill, that it was going to make sure the small business community knew about it. I know in my own community I sent at least five small businesses to the local banking institutions. I can tell you five for five, they came away with no help at all from the banking community. Either the banks did not know about it or they did not care to know about it and this government was sitting when it made that commitment.
The second thing I noticed-and then I am going to come immediately to the bill because it is relevant-was that I thought it was a pretty productive day in the House. We were working together on a very good piece of legislation. However, in all of Canada there was only
Government Orders
one small news story on the very important legislation we passed that day, legislation that would give hope to a lot of small business people and a lot of people that had not even started their businesses but wanted to. That is what it was designed for.
I forget what newspaper carried the story, but in my city the only paper that covered it was the Corriere Canadese which covered it in Italian. That is important as we have a large Italian community in our city, about
700,000	Italians, but it was not covered by The Toronto Star, The Toronto Sun or The Globe and Mail. It was good news. It was a positive story and the press never covered it. This is the reason why I say to the government that it has to promote the Small Businesses Loans Act.
It is a specific example of the opposition working with the government because it is legislation that will help put people back to work, it is going to be something that could help create more jobs.
Today we have before us Bill C-112. It is sort of the son of the son of GST, three years later. It is another attempt at refining a tax that has done a great deal to dampen and suppress entrepreneurial spirit and consumer confidence in this country. I know in my own riding it has practically cut the restaurant business in half, not to mention what it does to students who tend to work thenway through either high school or college by working in restaurants part time. They count on not only this type of work in the restaurant-tourism business but on the tips. It has just gutted the hopes for half-decent, part-time income for tens of thousands of university students right across Canada.
This poorly designed GST has brought further red tape to all the small business community in Canada, surprising for a Conservative government which tends to be a little bit more sensitive, which is supposed to be more sensitive to business. It has throttled people with this bureaucratic nightmare of a GST. Here we are three years later with some amendments, some refinements.
This bill that the government has put forward is proof positive of what we have been saying about the complexity, about the unfairness and about the inefficiency of the GST during the last three years. The government is now admitting, three years later, that what it had really was not that great.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
My leader three weeks ago said that this GST will be scrapped. Make no mistake about it, the GST will be scrapped if we are given the trust to run the Government of Canada.
When we talk about scrapping the GST, the most common question we hear from the other side, from the street or sometimes from journalists is: What are you going to do to replace the $15 billion worth of revenue that the GST delivers? What is the Liberal Party of Canada going to do to generate the $15 billion?
For starters, this GST has done much damage to the retail business in this country. It has done much damage and caused much unemployment and welfare. Yes we have had a world recession, but this GST has exacerbated the confidence problem in this country. Therefore, when we talk about revenue this tax has caused a situation where our welfare and unemployment insurance payments, including interest rates, are over $30 billion.
If you developed a fair tax system in this country and if you put 400,000 or 500,000 people back to work you could find $15 billion within four or five months, not to mention the fact that we would start giving people back their dignity. We have to understand that there are close to two million people in this country who are out of work.
I cannot imagine a single member of Parliament in any party in this House of Commons wanting to defend the status quo in terms of tax law in this country. In fact I have not met a member of Parliament who believes that the tax act of this country is fair, simple or efficient. We all agree that this 2,400-page document, with its rules and regulations and its exceptions and its exceptions to exceptions, is no longer intelligible. This tax act, combined with the GST, has caused an underground economy of cash deals in this country. Experts estimate that right now there are over $100 billion of cash transactions in this country.
Why do people want to do cash deals? They want to do cash deals because they feel that the current tax system is unfair. Everyone in the country feels it is unfair. Because the GST has exacerbated that feeling of unfairness people collaborate with one another. They say "I will paint your house at half the price if we can do a cash deal". He will pay GST on half that amount because on a cash deal he would not pay any GST. Sometimes it is half
cash and maybe a third on an invoice so they pay the GST on the smaller amount. All kinds of schemes are going on in this country right now. That underground cash economy is just out of control.
The question comes to us in opposition: If you are going to scrap the GST what are you going to do to find $15 billion? For the twentieth time in this House of Commons I am going to plead with this government to look at reforming this system. There is an alternative to the GST and there is an alternative to this current tax act. You do not need to defend the status quo. This is just one option-there are many-and it is the single tax.
People want accountability. When you have a tax act where there is absolutely minimal accountability, and that is reinforced by the GST because of the underground economy, you have to look at the single tax. What is the single tax? The single tax system essentially would say we have to stop running every aspect of the economy through the tax act of Canada. Right now, for every sector of our economy, whether it is the forestry sector, the mining sector or the environment, we run all kinds of tax preferences, special preferences, through the tax act. We have tax loopholes in this tax act that go back 20 years that have not been reviewed in terms of accountability.
Just this year, two offshore drilling projects cost the taxpayers of Canada close to $2 billion. They did not create hardly a single job in Canada because of a loophole that was buried in that tax act from 20 years ago. All of those tax preferences should be flushed out of the tax act. If any sector of our economy wants a tax grab or a tax expenditure it should go to the line department, justify it and link it to job creation.
Right now there is very little linkage, if any, in terms of the preferences in here and how they are meeting job creation possibilities.
If we had a single tax system in which we basically asked people on the corporate side for 20 per cent of their net income and the same on the personal side-after allowances were made for seniors, families with children, and charitable donations, and we could keep the RRSP structure in place-then that would empower people and get them back on stream. Right now people are running away from the tax act of this country because they can no longer understand it. It is so complex.
March 12, 1993

The GST has exacerbated that. No matter how many amendments or refinements the government brings in on this bill it cannot make a silk purse out of a sow's ear. The GST is a sow's ear and the Canadian public is never going to accept it. One of the reasons the Canadian public is never going to accept this bill is because the government introduced it at a time when people were on their knees. They were crying out for some hope, looking to the national government for some confidence and it threw this bill at them.
Going back to the single tax, if we have a system which everyone in the country feels is fair then people work harder, they work smarter, and productivity levels rise. When productivity levels rise then that is how jobs are created.
If we could put 400,000 or 500,000 people back to work in the next four to five months and if we could regain some of that underground economy, cut it in half to about $30 billion or $40 billion, just think of the amount of revenue that would bring to this Treasury.
I hear criticism and people asking: Where are you going to get the $15 billion? That is a defeatist attitude. Does the minister want to defend the status quo?
This is going to be a great six months, because I love people who defend the status quo. The status quo is a GST that has exacerbated the underground economy in this country to the point where it is over $100 billion. The Minister of Transport knows that. There are two million people out of work and he wants to continue to promote the status quo.
Is the government saying that it cannot do better? The government is essentially saying it cannot improve on the status quo. Canadians do not believe that for a second. They do not believe for a second that we cannot regain some of the underground economy. They do not believe for a second that there are not ways to put people back to work.
The problem with this government is that it talks a good deal but it has no action plans. I refer specifically to that Small Businesses Loans Act where the Minister of Finance committed to do something about it and the
Government Orders
minister for small businesses committed to do something about it. I called the department this week and it said not to start promoting the Small Businesses Loans Act right now because it has not even gone through the Senate, which the government controls.
That is how much this government really cares about the small business community in this country. The government has this smug and arrogant attitude that it cannot improve on the status quo. Canadians are not going to accept it. They want a debate on tax reform.
I am not saying that the single tax is the panacea for this country. I am not saying that it is the only alternative. I am saying that when there are $40 billion worth of tax grants to business in here, which have been mostly put in by lobbyists and people that have been able to influence the Department of Finance, and if the government refuses to review these from time to time and not have some form of accountability then how can it say it is serving the taxpayers of Canada?
Is it telling me that in $40 billion worth of tax grants there is no room to flush some of those out or review them? Does the minister agree with the offshore drilling that happened with two oil companies last year, which cost the taxpayers of Canada $2 billion? How many jobs were created in Canada? That is defending the status quo.
I think it is wrong. Canadians know it is wrong and they want a fair, simple and efficient system. Did you know, Madam Speaker, that 80 per cent of the tax returns filed in this country had to be returned because of mistakes made in the system. Does this government want to defend that? If it sits there, smiles and says that it cannot do better then that is defending the status quo. Canadians want better. We need better and we can do better.
The government says that we are not constructive, that when something good comes along in this House we do not co-operate. The government fooled me two weeks ago because I really believed that this government was sincere and serious about trying to get credit for the
960,000	small businesses in this country.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
This government is not sincere when it makes a commitment to help small business. It brings a bill before this House, gets it before the House, we co-operate, and then nothing happens. That is wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext: That's not the case.

The member for Peterborough says that is not the case, but I can tell the House that it is. We co-operated. The member knows it, he was there. I called the minister's office on Monday and I do not want to repeat the answer in this House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext: Put it on the record.

I will put in on the record. I was told that I should not be promoting that bill right now because it has not gone through the Senate. Does the hon. member for Peterborough agree with that? He does not believe that. Do not tell me that the member was not in his riding last week tiying to promote and help small business. He was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext: It's not proclaimed, but it's through the Senate.

Another excuse. This is the GST government, the defenders of the status quo and it makes these nice announcements before Christmas about the Small Businesses Loans Act. What a great bunch of teasers we have here. They are a great bunch of teasers. They come in today and talk about simplifying the GST; 350 pages of simplification.
In this country today there is a crisis of confidence. We have to do something in order to get the entrepreneurial spirit of this country moving again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext: You better get your party together.

This is what happens when a government has been around for 10 years and we try to make a point on behalf of those people in our community who are crying out for help right now, the 960,000 small business people. We try to make a constructive point on the fact they are not operating the Small Businesses Loans Act, that they are not actioning it, and they come back with smug, arrogant remarks. Instead of making smug, arrogant remarks, why do they not go to their Minister of Finance and their minister for small businesses and do something about it? They are in charge. Why do they not ask them to live up to the legislation that went through this House?
This is one of the reasons people have lost trust in the government. The government has lost its feeling for the
pain out there in the community. It has lost feeling for the fact that two million people right now are crying out for help. They want work. They want more jobs. It is not right to laugh. I am not treating this issue lightly. It is serious.
We have a situation today where the government wants us to support a bill to refine the GST. I am totally opposed to the GST. It is an inefficient, unfair tax. Small businessmen despise the GST. They want it replaced. They definitely want to make sure we do it in a responsible way. We cannot just snap our fingers and pull something out of the hat. There has to be a serious debate on tax reform, but they do not want us to defend the status quo which the Conservative government wants to defend. We are not going to defend the status quo. There is no way. There is absolutely nothing that could ever make me change my attitude toward the GST.
For the last three years I have seen the pain. I have watched people lose their businesses. I have watched retailers lose their stores. I have seen people lose their homes. A leadership change does not matter. It does not matter whether it is the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport or the Minister of National Defence. This is the GST government. Two million people out there are in pain and have been in pain for the last three years. They are not a mirage. They are real.
Believe me, the people who are working care as much and more about the people who are not working. They think if they ignore the two million unemployed that the ten million or eleven million who are working will support what they are doing to the others. They are making a mistake. It is not going to happen.
There are alternatives to defending the status quo. The status quo is unacceptable when we have over $100 billion in underground economy. The Auditor General said last year that most Canadians could not even understand the tax forms.
I am totally opposed to the bill. I cannot wait for the next election when the GST will be the singular issue hanging over this government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I join with my colleague who has just spoken to speak out as strongly as I can against Bill C-112, an act to fine tune the goods and services tax. That is what it is all about.
What will the people of Canada say when they see this document containing hundreds and hundreds of pages to fine tune the GST? It is already an impossible task for most people to handle. This is what makes small business operators, people running small firms, shake their heads in disbelief. An effort to improve the tax, from the government's point of view, is good news, but it cannot improve a tax that does not make any sense. It cannot improve a bad tax by introducing in the House of Commons hundreds of pages of detailed changes. That is not the way to deal with the GST. There is only one way for the country to deal with the GST, that is to scrap it as soon as possible to allow people to get on with rebuilding the economy.
What would you replace it with?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend on the government benches asks me what we would replace it with. I would ask him to take the time to read the economic recovery report presented by the federal New Democratic Party. It lays out in very specific detail the set of alternatives to the goods and services tax. I tell my hon. friend opposite that because of the GST and a whole range of government policies regarding taxation there is absolutely no faith at all in this country in the tax system of Canada. People have long since abandoned any hope that it is fair, just and equitable. They know this is a tax system dedicated almost exclusively to serving the wealthiest people of this country and the very largest corporations of Canada.
The best example of that is what the government introduced in the House a few days ago: a special tax loophole for the wealthiest families of Canada. The tax loophole was originally introduced in the early 1970s by the Liberal government of the day. It provides for
Government Orders
tax-free family trusts. By rolling money into a family trust no income tax is paid for 21 years. The 21 years under the Liberal administration was about to run out. Now the government steps in and says that it has a new twist to it. It is going to continue the tax gift to the richest people of Canada, to the richest families of this country, and they will not be paying any taxes until their children die.
In other words, the $70 billion in these special family trusts is not being taxed. That is wrong. That is unjust. That is unfair. That is why the people of Canada have lost complete faith that the government has any intention of trying to bring in a fair and just tax system. That is only one example.
Today, as we speak to this bill in the House of Commons, there are thousands and thousands of individuals with incomes over $50,000 a year who do not pay a single penny in income tax, not a single cent in income tax. There are hundreds of people whose incomes are over a quarter of a million dollars a year who do not pay one penny in income tax, to say nothing of people who make $100,000 and pay $10 in income tax.
It is an unjust system. It is an unfair system. It is a system the people of Canada have long since jettisoned in terms of being a reasonable system. Day by day by day the government makes it worse. Family trusts to give a tax loophole to the wealthiest people of Canada are ridiculous. The people of Canada are disgusted. That is why the minute there is an election call the Conservative benches across the way will be literally jettisoned as those people become new kinds of Tories. We will call them migratories, as Tories migrate away from Parliament Hill.
The GST, special tax breaks for the largest corporations and special tax breaks for wealthy people have turned Canadians into a population that has lost confidence in the tax system. Consequently much of our economy has moved underground. The best estimate we have is something in the neighbourhood of $100 billion annually in transactions that are untaxed because they are underground, they are on a barter system, they are on a cash system and no records are kept. Imagine if those $100 billion of annual transactions were taxed at the regular level of taxation. It would take care of our deficit. The deficit of this country alone would be dealt with on that one aspect alone, the $100 billion now in the underground economy.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
No wonder we are in such difficulties. No wonder we have a deficit problem. No wonder we have a debt problem. People have lost complete faith in our tax system.
Here we have the government's effort to simplify the tax system. If people are watching television today and hear us saying that this is a way to simplify our tax system it is no wonder that people have lost faith not only in this government but in a tax system as it is presently constituted.
However this bill deals specifically with the GST. One of the things it does is stated in clause 211. What clause 211 states is that information about the GST is to be kept secret from the people of Canada. It bars information about the GST. Therefore under the freedom of information legislation when we try to get information about how the GST is being handled in the country we will be barred from that information.
I ask the government members opposite: What is it that you are trying to hide? How can you support legislation that keeps valuable information about the GST from the people of Canada? What is it that you are trying to hide? I think these are fair questions and perhaps at the end of my presentation I can ask some of my hon. friends across the aisle to explain that. Why would you support legislation that keeps information about the GST from the Canadian public? Presumably you have a good reason and I am looking forward to hearing your speeches later. That is one clause.
The bill goes on and on. For example, one of the clauses covers yoghurt. It states that if you buy six containers of yoghurt you will not have to pay the GST. There is another clause relating to bull semen. It states that if you pay GST on bull semen it is refundable. For all the people who are interested in purchasing bull semen this is great news, the GST will be refundable. That is probably a good provision if you are a cattleman.
What about reading? Why do we have GST on reading material? Why do we have GST on children's story books? I look forward to hearing my friends across the way explaining, when they speak today, why they support one of the only tax systems in the entire world that taxes children's books, that taxes the Bible and that taxes
reading material. Why would people support a tax regime that does that? Why would they not at least now, when they are supposedly improving the GST, bring in legislation that would exempt reading material so that we can encourage people to read and work to fight against the high rates of illiteracy in this country?
Madam Speaker, you might detect a certain anger in my voice. I am angry because I have just spent two weeks in my constituency visiting people who operate small businesses, small retail stores, small manufacturing firms-
Theatrical firms.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, as a matter of fact, as my hon. friend calls out, a number of organizations involved with the arts have just been informed they are going to have their arts funding slashed. Is this not an intelligent approach to take to the arts organizations across Canada, to slash budgets for another year, after years and years of reducing their budgets, now to make them almost totally inoperable? I am pleased that my hon. friend reminded me of that.
As I visited business after business there was one common concern raised at every single visit. I cannot recall a single firm I visited that did not have this to say. They said: "As our federal representative do what you can to have this government reverse its position on the GST and drop this tax because of what it is doing to our business".
It is not the only problem that businesses face but for many it is the straw that breaks their backs. It is the reason that people lose their homes, it is the reason that families break up, it is the reason that there are thousands and thousands of bankruptcies every month in this country. One of the critical reasons is the GST. It puts the cost beyond what is reasonable. It eliminates those extra few customers that make the difference between a successful business and an unsuccessful business.
In conclusion, as we break for Question Period, I want to say on behalf of my party that we will oppose this legislation. We will oppose it as strongly as we can because even by changing the GST we cannot make this bad tax a good tax.
March 12, 1993

Madam Speaker, Canadians had just reason to feel pride last night after the greatest day in Canadian figure skating history. Not since our own Otto Jelinek and his sister Maria along with Don Jackson won 31 years ago have Canadians won both the pairs and the men's world championships.
Following Isabelle Brasseur and Lloyd Eisler's victory in pairs, Elvis Stojko skated almost flawlessly to claim a silver medal in the men's championship.
My pride and the pride of everyone in central Alberta was absolutely unlimited as Kurt Browning clinched his quad, a fourth world championship.
Four times I have had the pleasure of rising in this House to share our pride and congratulate Kurt Browning. He is an outstanding athlete, a fierce competitor and a proud Canadian. Kurt not only expresses his pride in Canada but by his skill and his actions he brings pride to this country. I am sure that all members of the House of Commons join me in congratulating Isabelle and Lloyd, Elvis and Kurt. They are the best in the world.
Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am concerned about Canada's ability to sustain our current level of peacekeeping operations. In the past five years more peacekeeping operations have been approved than in the previous 40 years. There is every indication that this trend will continue as ethnic tensions throughout the world increase along with the inability of smaller countries to cope.
Canada has 4,700 peacekeepers deployed around the world in 15 different locations. The size and scope of operations are increasing dramatically. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is correct. There were fewer women working in the work force in the month of February. We do not like to see that at all, though I must point out to her that there were
35.000	more working by the end of February than there were a year ago. This is a one-month drop, but the record over the last number of months has shown that it has increased.
I cannot explain the reasons for that. I am sure there are reasons that drop in the month of February took place. Unfortunately a lot of the part-time jobs that take place over the December-January months for Christmas and for sales in January disappear in February. I am sure that has something to do with it.
I agree with her that is a major problem, but this government is spending a tremendous amount of money, well over $3 billion, on training and retraining to try to get people into the work force with the skills they need for the jobs available today.
The hon. member knows, if she read it this week, that the help-wanted index is up rather significantly. Employers are now starting to look for employees. There are some very good signs in the economy. I believe we will see a marked improvement in employment as this year progresses and as the economy improves.

Madam Speaker, we also know that many of these single parents, women in particular, are working in jobs in the service industry that are low paying and they are hurting very badly.
It is also a fact that the unemployment rates are highest among single parents: 16.8 per cent unemployment for women led families and 15.7 per cent for male led families. That is far above the national average. We know this is caused mainly by an inflexible job market.
Why is this government failing to develop coherent policies that will empower these people to break this cycle of poverty?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can speak fairly authoritatively about what goes on in my community in the city of Brampton in the region of Peel where in fact there are very significant ongoing programs for single parents to get them back into the work force, training programs together with support for day care while the single parents are out working.
These programs are ongoing. I know they are taking place across this country. I can speak more authoritatively about the ones in my area because I keep a very close eye on them. As a matter of fact we are meeting with the region of Peel this afternoon to cover a number of these subjects.
That is a great concern. There is no question about it. There are programs in place, as the hon. member knows, in which the federal government funds the provinces very significantly when it comes to social assistance, trying to get people off social assistance, back into the training market and rnto the job market. Those programs are ongoing and will continue to be ongoing because they are a priority of this government.

Madam Speaker, U.S. President Clinton has recently stated that he will not ratify the North American free trade agreement unless substantive parallel agreements are made, including an environmental accord.
Is the minister or whoever is answering for the Minister of the Environment aware that through articles 301, 309, 310, 314, 315, 708 and annex 702.1 of the proposed NAFTA agreement and article 2201.9 of the harmonized coding system Canadian waters are treated as a commodity of trade and are exempted from environmental safeguards?
March 12, 1993

Will the minister seize this opportunity, an opportunity presented by President Clinton, to press for an irrevocable exemption for the export of Canadian waters under NAFTA?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)

I do not know if the member has read the agreement or a researcher gave him those numbers, but let me just read a very brief clause in the agreement, which says: "For greater certainty nothing in this act or the agreement, except article 401 of the agreement, applies to water. In this section water means natural surface and ground water and liquid in gaseous or solid state but does not include water packaged as a beverage or in tanks".
NDP members went through this export of water under the free trade agreement. They were shot down then and they are going to be shot down again under NAFTA.

God knows that in the past the government said it would not sell Air Canada and all sorts of other things that it changed in the future. The NAFTA allows water to flow. The government knows that.

It is one of the changes we are not asking for to make sure that generic drugs can be sold cheaply to consumers and to hospitals right across this country.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, my question is directed to the Minister of State for the Environment.
As she knows, the levels of ozone, the atmospheric gas that filters harmful ultraviolet radiation, reached historic lows over Canada this winter and are likely to remain significantly below normal at least until the fall. The trend is posing a threat to the health of Canadians, particularly in relation to skin cancer.
My question is this: What is the minister doing to assure the public that the government is taking the necessary steps to protect the ozone layer and thus the public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I think it would be helpful to tell my colleague what we expect the situation to be over the next few months, during the summer, if we ever get summer here.
The ozone depletion this summer is expected to be just slightly greater than observed in the last few years. Summertime values will be between 3 per cent and 7 per cent below the pre-1980 normal.
As the hon. member knows, we started a system of providing information about the ozone layer and ultraviolet radiation to Canadians so they could have that information. I would certainly suggest they take advantage of it and take precautionary measures to keep out of the sun when there are conditions that are particularly dramatic during the summer.

March 12, 1993
Oral Questions
I know my hon. colleague is aware of the fact that Canada has been the leader in promoting the international protocol. In Montreal last year, again we played a very active role in putting forward and strengthening that international protocol. In fact at that meeting the protocol was strengthened and the agreement that has been reached at Copenhagen calls for-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think we are getting into a speech now and the hon. minister will agree with me.

Madam Speaker, while the protocol, as the minister says, has been strengthened, one of the dangerous chemicals which is damaging the ozone layer is methyl bromide.
Methyl bromide has been banned in Holland and will be banned in the United States by the year 2000.
My supplementary question is this: Why is the government of Canada so hesitant in protecting the public and not acting in banning methyl bromide?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague mentions methyl bromide which was one of the issues considered in Copenhagen.
As a party to the accord that was reached, Canada supports the initiatives put forward in the protocol. We will be reducing the use of methyl bromide by 1995 down to the levels it was prior to 1991. We will be committed to recover, recycle and reclaim methyl bromide and to reduce emissions. Canada, as one of the partners around the world, will be ensuring that we all work in a concerted fashion to ensure that this does not continue to be a contributing cause to ozone depletion.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Public Works.
In his economic statement last December the Minister of Finance froze to 1990 levels all grants in lieu of taxes the government pays municipalities on its properties across Canada. A great number of these government properties are located in the national capital region.
Does the minister intend to rescind this unfair freeze on grants in lieu of taxes or does he intend to freeload on the increased cost of municipal services and bully the rest of the property owners in the national capital region into paying for the shortfall?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
On the contrary, Madam Speaker, we are hoping to find an equitable way to cope with the escalation in the costs to the government because of the rapid increase in grants in lieu assessments.
This has been done across the country under different methodologies. We are hoping as a result of meetings which we will have with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and other people that we will be able to find an equitable and consistent way to restructure the process. We are not trying to bully anyone and to the extent that we can we would like to try to be as equitable as possible under the constraints of the freeze.

Madam Speaker, the minister seems to have no immediate plans for dealing with the freeze.
The Ottawa-Carleton regional government recently approved a report by the province of Ontario which reassessed all property categories in the region. The regional government was aware of the implication that federal properties would yield about 3.4 per cent less in revenue in 1993. Will the government accept or reject this new lower assessment of its properties in Ottawa-Carleton?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister of Public Works

The point is that we do have this constraint and we do have this freeze. We are trying to cope with it as best we can and as equitably as we can until we can get a better methodology across the country that will be consistent and will reduce this rapid escalation in grants in lieu.
March 12, 1993

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and it concerns Panarctic's proposed dumping of 400 tonnes, or 800,000 pounds, of scrap metal into the Arctic Ocean.

March 12, 1993
Oral Questions
The government has a policy, the Arctic environmental strategy, for which this minister is responsible. It is supposed to protect the Arctic environment and fully accommodate the views of the aboriginal people. Given the absolute and total opposition of the Inuit to this proposed dumping, how can the minister allow it to proceed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I heard the Minister of State for the Environment respond to this question yesterday. She indicated that an appropriate environmental screening of this project was conducted under the provisions of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act and the environmental assessment process.
I was disturbed to learn that we might permit the dumping of such a large amount of steel into Arctic waters. I know the Department of the Environment is similarly concerned. I am told there were public meetings in Resolute before the permit was authorized. In view of the concern that has been expressed by northern leaders, I am told there will be meetings with community representatives to further review those concerns and to see if further appropriate steps are necessary.

Madam Speaker, having an environmental assessment review would be welcome news but the first preference of northerners is to see that these metals are removed to the south from where they came.
Has the government rejected the option of totally removing this garbage from the north?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I could respond to that.
I understand a number of options have been looked at as to what can be done. One of the requirements of Panarctic is that it clean up its site. That is under the legislation.
Certainly other options were looked at. Land disposal was looked at but given the conditions of permafrost this really was not a feasible option.
The option of transporting these materials south was examined. However, it would cost I understand something in the order of well over $1 million to do that and it was obviously considered excessive considering the situation involved.
As my colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has indicated, there will be further meetings about this. The bottom line is we want to ensure that any disposal is environmentally safe. Certainly the information we have would indicate that it would be safe but obviously further consultations will be under way.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I would like to inquire about the policy of his department with respect to liability arising from large construction and engineering projects on Indian lands where debts remain unpaid.
Many suppliers and contractors presume that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is essentially a guarantor of Indian financial commitments when the funds are advanced by his department. I would like to understand what his policy is, both in the ethical and in the legal sense.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is a very important question raised by the hon. member for Fredericton-York-Sunbury and one which other members have also asked me about.
I should begin by indicating that the majority of the bands which are administered across Canada by chiefs and councils handle their own financial arrangements, both their O and M funding and the capital funding they administer, often under multi-year operating budgets. We call them alternative funding arrangements.
The majority of these communities and their leadership pay their bills and meet their financial obligations. There are exceptions. Our position is both legally and morally that in the spirit of the self-government ethic that First Nations are seeking, the minister of Indian affairs and the government should not guarantee bills which are not paid.

March 12, 1993
Routine Proceedings
There are remedies through the courts and the legal system. It is important for contractors and those who do business with aboriginal communities to realize that they are dealing as they would with any other commercial entity. They are dealing in a situation where contract law must be respected and where it is not, the remedies are to be found through normal legal recourse, notwithstanding my concern that native leaderships live up to their obligations.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I assume the bill that is about to be introduced is the new borrowing bill which the government proposes to put to the House. If so, I would like to raise a point of order as to its procedural acceptability.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

Yes, very good, that is the bill that is about to be introduced.
Beauchesne's sixth edition, citation 595, states that:
The Crown, being the executive power, has the responsibility for the raising and spending of money. Acting through responsible Ministers, the Crown makes known to the Commons the financial necessities of government. The Commons grants such aids and supplies as are necessary to meet the demands of the Crown and provides through taxes and other sources of revenue the ways and means to meet the supplies that have been granted. The Crown, therefore, demands money, the Commons grants it and the Senate assents to the grant. The Commons does not vote any money except for the necessities of the country as defined by the Crown.
This particular bill is a borrowing bill. I assume that since it applies for the following year it is a borrowing bill for money for the new financial year. It has been the accepted practice in this House over the last decade and a bit that any such bill will be preceded by a budget or an economic statement that defines, within the meaning of Beauchesne's, the financial requirements of the Crown.
We have had no explanation as to any funding that may be required for borrowing purposes for the new financial year. Indeed, we were given conflicting answers as to whether there is going to be a budget. One day the Minister of Finance thinks there will be and the next day he is thinking about leadership possibilities instead. "


March 12, 1993

I want to look at the practice and I urge Your Honour to look at it also. I have done some research on this and I want to point out that in May 1980,1 have gone back that l'ar, following an economic statement in April, a borrowing bill was introduced in the House and that practice basically has been followed ever since.
On two or three occasions during the period of 1981 and 1982 the borrowing authority was included in a supply bill. The Speaker in 1981 ruled that it was improper to include the borrowing bill in a supply bill and had it removed. The government then reintroduced a new bill that gave borrowing authority. That practice has been followed ever since. It was tried again in 1982 in a supply bill but, again following complaints from the opposition, which is the government side at this time, the borrowing authority was removed from the supply bill and placed in another bill.
It has been a very consistent practice since that time that the borrowing bill be introduced separately and that it be introduced following an economic statement. I note for the record that in December of this year in the economic statement, borrowing authority was requested and that borrowing authority has been granted. It was additional borrowing authority for the current financial year. The borrowing authority for this year was originally requested in last year's budget on February 25 and the borrowing bill was in fact introduced immediately the budget was presented.
That has been the practice throughout the term of the government. It was the practice for the few years preceding this government coming to office. I could cite every bill.
I realize I am rising on a procedural point and it would be quite out of order for me to refer to incompetent management on the part of the government as the reason for this bill coming forward and I would not want to do that. It would also be wrong for me to suggest that the government in introducing the bill really does not know what it is doing or that it is busy in a leadership campaign. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to present some 9,000 signatures from constituents in the Peterborough federal riding and some of those surrounding it, calling on Parliament to consider major amendments to the Young Offenders Act. The majority of Canadians who signed this petition support equal treatment of criminal offenders but with legislated age shelters from criminal law for very young adolescents.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I submit approximately 525 signatures from people from Nepean, Gloucester, Ottawa, Hull and Gatineau, all communities in the Ottawa-Hull area.
These petitioners ask that Canada recognize rape as a war crime and they ask that Canada, through the United Nations, place more emphasis on resolving the deplorable situation in Bosnia and that Canada also communicate its displeasure to governments that promote and condone rape as a means of controlling their people as a weapon of war. For example, they mention again Bosnia, Croatia and India.

Madam Speaker, I have two petitions to present to the House today. The first petition is from residents of Essex-
Windsor and results from a petition drive across the constituency on a single day.
The petition calls the attention of the House to serious problems with the North American free trade agreement. It suggests that Canadians will lose more good jobs as a consequence of this agreement. It suggests that there will be further restrictions placed on the ability of Canada's various governments to assist Canadian industry. It suggests that there is no possibility of this being remedied through renegotiation.
The petitioners therefore call upon the House to reject the proposed North American free trade agreement and recommend to the government that it use the termination clause to end the U.S.-Canada free trade agreement.

The second petition I have also comes from my constituency. It is from a group of people who are very concerned about the serial killer board game which has been for sale in Canada. They are concerned that the laws of Canada do not deal with materials portraying torture, rape and murder as fun such as this game.
The petitioners therefore request Parliament to consider amending the Criminal Code so that violence and degrading material such as this serial killer board game can be kept from being distributed in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I too have a petition to present under Standing Order 36. There are slightly more than a thousand signatures on it from residents mainly of the Caroline-Rocky Mountain House area in my riding.
These people recognize that treaty rights entitle treaty Indians to preserve their traditional way of life including hunting, fishing and gathering. However, they point out that there are no bag limits in enforcement of hunting regulations for treaty Indians.
