speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (for the Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: that Bill C-102, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, the Excise Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Customs Act, the Criminal Code and a related act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to rise in the second reading debate on Bill C-102. It is an important bill which will give legitimate legislative effect to excise and tariff measures announced over the past 18 months.
The primary purpose of this bill is to implement a range of measures developed in response to serious problems Canada is facing in the areas of cross-border shopping, tobacco smuggling and tobacco tax evasion.
The bill also contains routine administrative and technical tariff changes. I will take a few minutes to review a few of the proposed changes in the legislation.
There is the broad series of measures to address the problems of tobacco smuggling and tax evasion. These measures were announced in February and April 1992.
Last week I was in my riding of Timiskaming-French River. I was talking to a grocery store owner. Until a very short time ago he averaged around $3,000 a week in cigarette sales. As we all know, the government and individual Canadians are very concerned about the health factors of smoking. This gentleman indicated it was not that individuals had stopped smoking. It was more a matter of the number of cartons of cigarettes coming into northern Ontario that had been smuggled across the border and the resulting tax evasion. His sales had dropped from $3,000 to something under $1,000 a week.
One regrettable aspect is that as a small businessman he has lost those sales but for Canadians there are all those taxes that were not paid. It is also regrettable that those cigarettes are still being purchased but they are being purchased at a very reduced price. In fact, it is somewhere around $4 a package under the table.
I applaud the government and the minister for taking these steps. For all Canadians, both those who may have the habit of smoking and those who do not, it is only fair that there should not be a break. There should not be an opportunity for the evasion of taxes by smuggling cigarettes into this country. I believe the proposals in both these budgets made a great step forward.
The adjustment to the excise tax rate on cigars to ensure that cigars are not taxed at a lower rate than cigarettes was announced in September 1991.
I really want to applaud the government and the finance minister on the elimination of the excise tax on ethanol and methanol portions of motor vehicle fuels. This is to encourage the development of fuels made from renewable feedstocks announced in the February 1992 budget. Again, I must say that it is a step in the right direction. Until this morning I was Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The individuals within the energy sector I have talked to over the past four and a half years were certainly very pleased to see that the taxation was taken from that.
March 12, 1993

Let me again refer to the great riding of Timiskam-ing-French River where we are looking now at the opportunities for getting an ethanol plant into that region. It is a region that certainly has a heavy base of agricultural products. We can look at using corn stock, grains, artichokes, sugar beets or whatever. We will also be able to use wood products and wood waste. That is another resource which is abundantly ready for us there.
Until the changes which took place in the February 1992 budget it was next to impossible to get anyone interested in investing in either ethanol or methanol. It certainly shows the vision of this government. It is a vision of ensuring the expansion and opportunity for the rural parts of this country. The fact is the finance minister listened to the people in the industry and the agriculture community in the rural parts of Canada. They stated that we had to have a resource that we could develop and enhance and that was ethanol and methanol.
Another item I would quickly like to review is the removal of customs duties from about 25 consumer products announced in the February 1992 budget to help address the cross-border shopping problem. That is another indication of how the government has listened to consumers and retailers, and to members of our caucus who were greatly concerned that changes be made.
Finally, there are the technical changes to the Customs Tariff to respond to industry concerns and meet our international obligations announced in the April 1992 economic statement, and some minor consensual amendments to the Criminal Code and Customs Tariff related to last year's gun control package.
I could certainly go on for a great deal of time on these subjects. The changes we are looking at are correct and are aimed at helping individual Canadians and those involved in the business side, or Canadians over-all, in regard to customs and excise.
Government Orders
I hope that we can see quick passage of Bill C-102 this afternoon because it certainly takes a correct step forward for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill which, as the hon. member for Timiskaming-French River said, is an act to amend the Customs Thriff, the the Excise Act, the Excise Tax Act, Customs Act, Criminal Code and a related act, one would have difficulty in speaking about this or any other method of taxation without the total perspective of where we are coming from.
I think most of us in the House at one time or another in the last four and one-half years have made many presentations, addresses and statements and have asked many questions in Question Period on the economy. I had some indication I would be speaking on this today and I want to put it into the perspective of where we are going with the business of raising money in Canada and spending it.
I thought I would go back to 1984 when the government took power. I want to have a look at some of its promises and aims and I want to look at how they may have been achieved. That might take a long time but I promise that it will not take as long as it might seem. I am not going to go through every budget. I am not going to read every single aim for every single year.
It might be instructive for the House to recall the first budget that the Conservative government put forward on November 8, 1984. I would like to put on the record what the four aims were. The first aim was to put our own fiscal house in order so that we limit and ultimately reverse the massive build-up in public debt and the damage and impact this has on confidence and growth.
The second aim was to redefine the role of government so that it provides a better framework for growth and job creation and less of an obstacle to change and innovation.
The third aim was to foster higher investment, greater innovation, increased international competitiveness and a positive climate for the growth and birth of new enterprise.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
The final aim was to bring about these changes in a way that is fair, open and consistent with the basic sense of compassion, tolerance and justice that is characteristic of Canadian society.
When that presentation was made the deficit was believed to be $35 billion and the national debt was $168 billion.
In the budget the following year, May 1985, the four aims were slightly different but in principle fairly similar. They are much shorter so I am going to read them as well. The first aim was to create a tax structure that gives greater encouragement to individual enterprises, risk taking, entrepreneurship and investment. The second aim was to improve the fairness and equity of the tax system. The third aim was to reduce the deficit in the short run through the imposition of temporary surtaxes. The fourth aim was to put in place a revenue structure that would generate resources growing slightly faster than the growth in the economy, thus providing continuing help in the reduction of the deficit over the medium term.
That was in 1985. The annual deficit was about the same at $35 billion, but the national debt had grown beyond $168 billion. I will spare the House going through every budget, 1986, 1987 and 1988. Those were years when growth was big. The country was growing and the western economies were growing. We went through 1989, 1990, 1991 and 1992. On December 3, 1992 the Minister of Finance, a new Minister of Finance, introduced his mini budget, as it was called, which said how terrible it was that the deficit was still $35 billion and that the national debt, despite these great aims and despite the efforts in years of growth, had miraculously more than doubled from $168 billion to, at the time, around $450 billion.
I do not know where to go from here. This is the aim and it has been the same for eight and half years. Now we are told that we are not going to have a budget because there is a leadership race on. We are told that it probably would not be a good thing to introduce a budget. We might have a financial statement.
The reason we may have a financial statement is the same reason we had a mini budget in December. In the words of the finance minister, it was to bolster the faith of the international community which wants to kick us out of the G-7 because of our deficit and debt record. The finance minister says we might have to have some
kind of a financial statement and another projection of what the deficit and debt is going to be because we do not want the international community to think that we cannot pay our bills.
I am not surprised that at a minimum the finance minister would want to reassure the international community that we can pay our bills because when the budget was introduced in 1984 we owed roughly 42 per cent of what we made. Our accumulated debt was around 42 per cent of what our Gross Domestic Product was. More important, we owed only 9 per cent of that amount to foreigners.
Today we owe close to 70 per cent of what we make. Our accumulated debt is 70 per cent of the goods and services that are produced in this country, but more important, 30 per cent of that is owed to foreigners. Is there any reason why they should not be concerned that we may not be able to pay our bills? Is there any reason why, at a minimum, as the finance minister says, that we should not have some kind of a statement, never mind the leadership race? We owe it not only to Canadians but to the international community. We owe it 30 per cent of what we make.
We owe the international community a statement to reassure it, to tell it that maybe the deficit will be the same as it was eight and a half years ago and that the national debt will be a little bit more than 70 per cent of what we are worth. We are going to tell it not to worry because we are going to do something that is incredible. We are not sure what that is, but we certainly look forward to it whenever that day happens.
This is serious stuff. Somewhere in Vancouver, I have not seen this, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps you have, I am told there is a clock in Vancouver called the doomsday clock. It shows how much our national debt is increasing. According to this clock it goes up over $1,000 a second. Imagine making that kind of money. That money is owed to foreigners.
I am as concerned as the government is about this problem. On this side of the House we have been criticizing its policies. In general terms one would have hoped that when the economy was increasing and booming in those years I have mentioned, 1984 to 1988-89, the government would have been able, as its aims were in the two years I have mentioned, to reduce the debt and deficit. It was not able to do that.
March 12, 1993

If the government was unable to reduce the annual deficit and the accumulating debt when times were good and when we were making more, when our gross domestic product was increasing at roughly 3 per cent a year on average over that period of time, how in the name of everything holy with the world recession and our own recession, which at the government's own admission was made in Canada and exacerbated by the ugly and hated goods and services tax, are we going to be able to reduce it? The government has run out of tactics. It has run out of tricks. Now the only thing the government does is blame it on the Liberals, after eight and one-half years.
Maybe it could try to after the first or second year, but as a Liberal I certainly do not believe that I should take credit for something that the government could not do in eight and one-half years.
As if to add insult to injury, all this took place when Canadians were subjected to 38 tax increases. I like numbers because numbers are objective. I distinguish numbers from statistics. These numbers that I have in front of me indicate things like compassion for the individual, tolerance and justice, job creation, growth, a better tax system, temporary surtaxes.
In 1984 personal income taxes as a percentage of total budgetary revenues for the Government of Canada represented 41.2 per cent. This is a Statistics Canada figure. Last year that figure increased to 47.7 per cent. That is an increase over this eight and one-half-year period that I am talking about, this critical period, of 15 per cent for individuals.
What happened to big businesses? What happened to corporations? The percentage of the budgetary revenues they paid went from 13.2 per cent of the national collection in 1984 down to 7.2 per cent last year. That is a decrease of 50 per cent.
I am still talking about taxes. I am talking about the effect that this goods and services tax and the 37 other taxes have had on Canadians. 1990 and 1991 were the last two years for which I can get figures. In 1990 individuals in Canada paid $92.7 billion in taxes. The following year they paid $104.6 billion, which in any man's mathematics is an 11.5 per cent increase in one year in what individuals paid. What about corporations? In 1990 corporations went from $14.6 billion down to
Government Orders
$12.4 billion. In other words they had a decrease of 15 per cent.
I could give more figures but I wanted to use those two examples to let everyone know that the Canadian individual on surtax, on real tax, on income tax, on petroleum tax, on cigarette tax, is taxed to death. We are now at the point where if an individual is taxed any more he or she will not be able to contribute to the economy in the best possible efficient manner.
This is hard to explain without graphs but basically we have passed the break-even point where individuals contribute efficiently to the economy. In other words they are paying so many taxes they will not be able to have disposable income to spend in the economy so that the economy can be assisted and helped.
Add to that phenomenon the $100 million that we are losing through the underground economy. That is an estimate. It could be $200 million, it could be $75 million, but it is a lot of money.
This is all related to putting people back to work. I believe the government has attempted in its policies to rectify this serious situation, has tried to create growth and has tried to better the unemployment situation but it has not succeeded. If it were to create a better situation for jobs it would certainly better the situation for the debt and the deficit.
The figures that I have say that for every 100,000 unemployed Canadians getting back into the work force, the federal government would collect $360 million in income tax, providing we do not increase the income tax any more.
For the same 100,000 people getting back to work the government would save $900 million in support payments, welfare and UI that it now costs. For every
100,000	people that go back to work the government in fact is better off by $1.2 billion. If we put a million people back to work, which is three-quarters of what we have unemployed right now, basically we are looking at $12 billion that would help with the deficit this year alone.
Last year we had 77,000 corporate, mostly small business, and individual bankruptcies. That is incredible. It is a record high in a year when the jobless rate was at a record high, over 1.5 million Canadians without work.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
It is not me saying that. It is not this side of the House saying that. In a recent CFIB, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, survey conducted in 1992 when concerns about taxes and regulation continued to be the dominant issues, of those people who were surveyed 82 per cent said their main concern was over taxes and 72 per cent said their concern was on regulations. Eighty-eight per cent stated dissatisfaction with the federal government's progress and expenditure reduction that was promised on November 8, 1984.
As I said in this House before, people turn to me and say I am from Newfoundland and that I should know the reason we cannot do anything with our deficit, that I should not have trouble understanding it. After all, a lot of money is spent supporting people on social services and unemployment insurance. Canada cannot afford to spend that kind of money on social programs any more. They are wrong. Not only are they a little bit wrong, they are dead wrong. They have not checked their figures. They have not done their homework.
Canada's social spending is one of the lowest in the world as a percentage of our gross domestic product. I am quoting Statistics Canada figures. Our social spending is 21.5 per cent of our gross domestic product and this compares with an average of 25.6 per cent, almost 20 per cent higher, for all the other industrialized countries in the OECD.
Many of the European nations that we have a lot of respect for financially, whose debts are much lower and whose financial management is considered to be more successful, have high standards of living and successful economies, spend considerably larger percentages of their gross domestic product on social programs. Let me give you some of the figures: Belgium, 37.6 per cent; Holland, 36.1 per cent; West Germany, 31.5 per cent; France, 29 per cent.
The only industrial countries in the world where social spending is lower than Canada's is the United States, with an expenditure of 20.8 percent and Japan at 17.5 percent. But I am not going to talk about Japan.
We know about the current debate concerning socialized medicine and medicare in the United States. A large proportion of their people cannot afford to be sick. The reason their bills get so high and that old age is such a problem in the United States is that when people are in their middle age they are afraid to go to see doctors because they cannot afford to pay the horrendous bill that is facing them, so they wait until it is absolutely
necessary to see a doctor when they are older. However, by the time they get to see the doctors they still cannot afford it but they have to go because they do not have a choice. When they get there the financial impact is disastrous.
I have relatives in the United States and they tell me that it is their children and in some cases their grandchildren who have to pay exorbitant sums of money, and I am talking about tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars, that in Canada would not cost you a penny other than your contribution in taxes.
Mr. Speaker, I say to you that whatever the reason for the almost incredible situation with debt and with our deficit we are in, it is not because of social spending.
I want to make this one point before I finish my presentation. I will give one example that I have been involved in to give the House some idea of what it means to the well-being of this country.
I am going to make reference to the EH-101 helicopter program. This is a program that is currently under a lot of fire and is being looked at from many angles. It has come under scrutiny in the last two months because of the Auditor General's report, because the minister showed some ambivalence toward it and because now defence analysts are looking under doormats and through cobwebs for every little thing here and there.
Some of the scrutiny is not exactly accurate, some of it is biased against the program. Certainly one of the jobs I have as defence critic is to sort out the wheat from the chaff. Quite frankly, I am disappointed that there are some areas where the articles written against the program are just not accurate. They are biased against the program. I do not think that is necessary and I do not support it.
On the expenditure of the money involved, the Minister of National Defence, and I hope she is not using this as a ploy, on three occasions that I am aware of and perhaps more has said in the House in opposition to our questioning of the expenditure on these helicopters at this time in our history and our economy that she does not understand what all the fuss is about because in 1990 everyone agreed that the EH-101 helicopter, the Merlin helicopter, was a suitable replacement for the Sea King. It was agreed by all members of the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs. This happened in 1990, and now she says: "I do not understand why all of a sudden you are now saying we have a problem with the program", quite apart from the fact that the geostrategic situation has changed tremendously
March 12, 1993

in the period we are talking about. The cold war was pretty cold in 1990.
However I want to focus on the point that I am making on the management of the economy of the country. The deficit at that time was projected to be around $18 billion that year. Let us say it was $20 billion. As 1993 is upon us and as this program is under scrutiny, the deficit is not $20 billion, the deficit is $34.5 billion. If the deficit were what the government had projected it to be in 1990, we could have had not this program but two and one-half of these programs at the same cost. I think that illustrates the difficulties one has in making projections and making promises and trying to do things you do not end up achieving.
Where are we spending money we do not need to spend? I just talked about the $100 million in the underground economy. I just talked about $12 billion if you put one million people back to work.
I was horrified in November when the Auditor General's report stated, and it was substantiated by the Auditor General himself, that hundreds of millions of dollars in corporate tax revenue was lost through offshore tax schemes.
When this first came out the finance minister himself-I was in the House when it happened and I am sure he was doing it with the best information he had-denied that was the case. He said there was something wrong, that we do not lose money through these offshore tax schemes. We tax everybody the same. He did not say that but that was the proposal, that was the information that was involved.
It was a couple of days later at a session of the public accounts committee where the finance officials admitted-I think it was a Tuesday after the Auditor General's report which I believe came out on Wednesday or Thursday of the previous week-they had checked their books and now believed that hundreds of millions of dollars were being lost.
Government Orders
In fact my hon. friend from Broadview-Greenwood suggested it was in the vicinity of $2 billion. Well you can add that $2 billion to the $12 billion and there is $14 billion. That is half the deficit right there.
There was $8 billion in grants and loans to businesses which the businesses themselves have said does not help them. Here is $8 billion more, add that to the $14 billion, that is $22 billion.
Where else do we go? Well, we have a cabinet. I do not make these decisions, it is an observation. We have 36 ministers with their staffs and the overheads to run this country. The United States with 10 times the population is run with 15 cabinet ministers. I suggest there might be some rather large savings there. Some might say I am nickel and diming. Well, I am up to $16 billion without even sitting down with a pencil and paper.
Let me mention another area. My colleagues have gone on about the goods and services tax. I am not going to drive that home any further, but I do want to say that at a time when the recession was with us, when the economy was bankrupt, the idea of a consumption tax that was not in harmony with provincial taxes would not have been introduced by anybody with any financial moxie whatsoever.
Not only did this government insist on doing it but it brought in extra senators, invoking a part of the Constitution that had not been used in 125 years at the cost to the taxpayer of around $30 billion.
I have only one other comment I want to make on the goods and services tax and the economic state that our country is in.
I find it passing strange, I really do, that the government could talk about a goods and services tax in the campaign election of 1988. It was not really identified as a goods and services tax, but was referred to by pessimists as a hidden tax. It was not discussed. It certainly was not introduced as a goods and services tax. It was going to be revenue neutral. It was just going to be a restructuring of things. We were not going to make any money on it. It was going to be simple.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
It is so simple that this morning 350 pages were introduced in this House to further simplify it. If that is simple I do not know what the government would consider complex.
My figures say that the manufacturers' sales tax was raised from 8.5 per cent to 13 per cent by this government. It was one of the 38 that I mentioned. It jacked it up and then complained about it. It said that it was too high. This government was the one that raised it, on the backs of the manufacturers. It was discussed in the House this morning.
The government said: "The goods and services tax will make up for that. We will just rearrange things". Then in the midst of the debate the government said: "No, what we will do is use the goods and services tax to help reduce the national debt and the deficit".
The aim was changed but the effect was the same. The manufacturers' sales tax took in $15 billion. Now we are told that the goods and services tax took in about the same: $15 billion. That may not have included the $1 billion or so it cost to introduce the tax. We do not know how much it cost. I would propose that with 350 pages of amendments and efforts to further simplify the goods and services tax we may never know how much it cost to introduce it.
There again is an area that causes great concern. There are other areas that I would like to speak about, such as the transfers to the provinces and the CAP for the wealthier provinces. I would like to discuss the reduction in transfer payments to Newfoundland. It is not a wealthy province and had relied on the federal government for 49 per cent of its income to run the province. That figure has now been reduced to 43 per cent. Over time it has cost the Newfoundland government somewhere in the vicinity of $800 million. This year alone the figure will be $150 million, which is 5 per cent of what it takes to run the whole province. The government cannot tell me that this is not causing a lot of difficulty to people who can least afford it.
I wanted to have on record these remarks on the economy in the context of this bill in front of us. I am sure as it comes up for discussion and further reference, up to and including third reading, and in the minds of those people who look at any subject that refers to taxes and the economy that they will have the macro-economic picture concerning raising taxes to run this country in mind.
I am sure that this side of the House will be ever cognizant of these measures in our resolution to put us back on track and to allow the country to move onwards and upwards in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a few comments on record with respect to Bill C-102.
It is a bill that was brought about partially in response to the bleeding of the Canadian economy across the border as a result of our high dollar, the goods and services tax and taxation that was perceived by Canadians, and rightfully so, to be too high.
The flood of people going across the border and purchasing their goods and services caused a lot of problems for Canadian retailers. From that perspective, I would suggest that there are parts of this bill that are positive for business people within my community and other border communities such as Grand Forks, Midway, Osoyoos and others where businesses directly felt that bleeding of the Canadian economy.
In this bill there are some 30 measures that reduce various tariffs on various goods coming into the country in an attempt to allow our entrepreneurs, our small business community and our retailers to compete a little more successfully against those businesses directly across the border in the United States.
Although it did little at the time when the problem was at its height it was a recognition that a problem was there and something had to be done. In that way I am pleased that some of these changes have been made to assist our small business community, hopefully making it a little more viable given the high number of bankruptcies we have had over the last two or three years within that same business community. Bankruptcy rates have been far in excess of anything we have witnessed in recent Canadian economic history.
One of the areas of the bill I would like to specifically speak on is that part which affects a specific part of the small business community. Some years back the government encouraged entrepreneurs to make bids on opening up duty-free shops along the border crossings into the United States to try to get a little bit more money
March 12, 1993

generated before people left the country and came back into the country.
Within my riding there is a very successful duty-free shop, the Osoyoos duty-free shop run by the Bissonette family. It also runs a similar duty-free shop over in the Cranbrook crossing, at what is called Kingsgate. These shops were set up across Canada. The various bidders on them spent a lot of time putting their bids together and spent a good deal of effort, time and money in setting up their shops once their successful bids were accepted by the government and set into place.
In speaking to other members of Parliament from all sides of the Elouse-Liberals, Conservatives, and New Democrats-who have border communities and dutyfree shops, I am told, and it is confirmed by those entrepreneurs operating the duty-free shops, that a good portion of the income of those shops comes from people leaving the country. As they leave the country to go down into the United States for a month, two months, or whatever, they will pick up their supply of Canadian cigarettes and Canadian alcoholic beverages and take them into the United States duty free.
What was proposed in February 1992, under the original section of this bill, was that because of the valid concern of the Canadian government over smuggling of tobacco products into Canada it had to do something to stem that tide. Canadian cigarettes were ending up duty free in the United States, being smuggled back into Canada and then sold, thereby undermining not only our small businesses but our tobacco manufacturers.
While I do not smoke myself and I would encourage others not to smoke because of a number of reasons- health, safety, and environmental-I also appreciate the right of those who so choose to have the availability of cigarettes for their consumption.
The Department of National Revenue turned its guns on the duty-free stores and said that the smuggling was taking place as a result of people taking cigarettes from the duty-free stores and bringing them back in. Subsequently that was found not to be the case.
A recent letter which I received on February 26, 1992 from the Frontier Duty-Free Association said: "A memo indicates that export of cigarettes and tobacco has increased from 3 per cent in 1986 to 14 per cent in 1991.
Government Orders
This is a rather considerable figure considering other commodities have increased considerably more. Also, please be aware that in 1986 there were only approximately 10 duty-free shops on the international border whereas now there are 35".
Last week an executive of one of the major tobacco companies in Canada said that of the total amount of cigarettes being exported out of Canada only 4 per cent of the total amount is being exported through duty-free shops, leaving 96 per cent being exported by other means. That shows the small amount that goes through duty-free shops.
The government backed off after negotiations with the duty-free associations and said that because of the co-operation of the duty-free associations across Canada in limiting the number of cartons of cigarettes and tobacco products any one person could take out of their shops it would back off on the duty. It did back off on the duty that was placed, and it was suspended on April 8,
1992.	As I understand it, in this bill the tax can still be imposed by Order in Council should the cabinet consider that action is warranted.
I think at this time it would be helpful to the House, to the minister and to the Department of National Revenue to hear the contents of a letter I received in November of last year from the Osoyoos duty-free shop in which the president, Denis Bissonette, sets out some of the problems involved within the duty-free association.
He states: "On behalf of the Frontier Duty-Free Association I wish to express my very serious concerns about the current efforts being made by the members of the departments of finance and revenue to legislate restrictions on sales being made from Canadian dutyfree shops.
Presently all Canadian duty-free operations are adhering to a one carton and two-tin limit on all sales of cigarettes and fine-cut tobaccos respectively. These items were voluntarily imposed by each Canadian dutyfree operator for the following reasons: one, to gain exemption from the $8 a carton export tax or equivalent from February 12, 1992 and therefore maintain at least some form of a level playing field with our U.S. competitors; two, to demonstrate to the various departments that the Canadian duty-free operators were not involved with the problem of tobacco smuggling into Canada.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
Even though the implementation of the export tax was subsequently suspended by our government the Canadian duty-free operators continue to hold true to their volunteered tobacco limits. This was done on the understanding that once officials from the departments of finance and revenue were reasonably convinced that Canadian duty-free operators were not involved with the tobacco smuggling problem discussions would be held to bring the tobacco sales limits to more constructive levels.
At meetings held with representatives of the departments of finance and revenue on June 23, 1992 and September 28, 1992 it was clearly stated by some of the officials present that they were satisfied that all Canadian duty-free shops were complying to the volunteered selling limits and that they now recognized that the Canadian duty-free shops were not part of the smuggling problem.
Therefore the question is why proceed with legislation to limit the sales from Canadian duty-free shops if it has been demonstrated and recognized that Canadian dutyfree shops are not part of the smuggling problem. At a time when the Canadian duty-free industry as a whole is facing significantly increased competition from the United States the only consequences of such restrictive actions will be to provide U.S. retailers with an additional competitive advantage and subsequent loss of millions of dollars in tourist revenue.
The Canadian duty-free industry plays a key element in the Canadian economy through its employment of hundreds of Canadian workers and the generation of substantial tax and revenue dollars to the federal and provincial governments. The vast majority of Canadian duty-free industry is composed of small to medium businesses owned by Canadian citizens.
The political agenda of our current government has been to energize and support Canadian small to medium businesses to stimulate the employment of Canadians and to promote exports in other countries. The current actions to legislate limits on the sales from Canadian duty-free shops directly contradicts such agenda. Therefore, on behalf of the Canadian Frontier Duty-Free Association I ask for your support on this most critical of issues to presently face our industry".
That sets out in capsule from what the position of the duty-free people is; that there is no need for the legislation. They are willing and have been co-operating and reporting to the revenue and customs departments any substantial increases in sales to any particular people. To proceed on anything that would unduly limit these entrepreneurs, or in fact force them out of the business or into bankruptcy would be wrong.
Let me move briefly to another area that has opened up by the very fact of this bill and the other bill before the House today. This was mentioned earlier by the hon. member from Newfoundland in his remarks. That is the loss of billions of dollars to the Canadian coffers as a result of the offshore tax havens. We have been talking about that in this party for a number of years. In last year's report the Auditor General confirmed that in his opinion hundreds of millions of dollars were leaking from the Canadian tax base as a result of offshore tax havens.
The response from the Ministry of Finance was that in the guise of competitiveness we had to allow these tax loopholes. It is interesting that when talking to Revenue Canada officials there appears to be a major rift between the Department of Revenue and the Department of Finance with respect to this. Revenue agrees it is a major problem. There is a major bleeding of our taxes through these loopholes. There are some 360 very large corporations using various tax loopholes to benefit their profits.
Revenue officials tell us that the loopholes could be closed without hurting our competitiveness. The competitiveness thing is simply a red herring. There would never and should not be taxation or double taxation of offshore income in Canada. If income is legitimately earned offshore and is brought back in and dividends are paid out to the shareholders or the corporation in Canada, there should not be taxation of that a second time if it has already been taxed in the other jurisdiction. Revenue Canada states that and I do not have a problem with that.
March 12, 1993

The key crunch is that Revenue Canada officials tell us that it is not hundreds of millions of dollars that are lost, it is billions of dollars. The member mentioned $2 billion. In fact, revenue officials have told me that it is probably higher than that. Billions of dollars per year are lost in taxes to these large corporations using their shell companies and paper transactions.
In two areas the loophole could be closed in what is called loss importation. That is where there are losses offshore, in offshore corporations. Under the present legislation those losses can be brought forward and offset against the profits of the corporation in Canada. That is a major loophole which amounts to hundreds of millions of dollars right there.
There is another one with Canadian source income that is allowed to be funnelled out through an offshore company. An example of that is the Canada Trust Co. case which is a fairly small one. I believe it is before the courts now. Approximately $30 million of mortgages guaranteed by CMHC were sold to a Shell company in the Netherlands. That company apparently then made the income from these CMHC guaranteed mortgages in Canada. Therefore it was income earned in Canada, taken offshore and declared as income of the offshore corporation and dividended back to the same company. The income lost in that particular case appears to be somewhere in the area of $3 million to $4 million. This is fairly small on the whole scale of things but it is an example of what I mean when I say that these tax loopholes could in fact be closed with major consequences.
Those types of things would help the totality of the Canadian economy. It would assist the regular taxpayer in understanding what is going on within the tax regime, that in fact there is a level playing field and that lower income earners are being treated the same as the huge multinationals and the wealthy corporations and taxpayers within Canada.
I just wanted to mention that and point out that there are many things we can do to try and increase the tax fairness in Canada, to try to ensure that we get back the credibility of our government and the credibility of our parliamentary system.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few comments with respect to Bill C-102. This bill of course
Government Orders
is seeking to enact several tax and tariff measures that have been announced recently.
Some of the measures are notable, for example those addressing tobacco smuggling and tax evasion. The bill also addresses the excise tax rate on cigars and other tariff reductions in order to reduce the cross-border shopping that has been a problem until recently with Canada's high interest rates and high dollar.
Although the bill has some good points, I submit it does not really solve the initial problem which is the fact that we have the GST in the first place. The government knows full well there are many things wrong with this tax. The tax has been a real burden on the economy. It has been difficult for our small business sector to adjust to the administrative costs of this tax. It has been difficult for consumers to put up with the extra financial burden caused by this tax.
The government would solve all problems at once by simply scrapping this tax, phasing it out, getting rid of it and imposing the kind of tax reform we have been requesting for some time. I think the GST is the real source of our misery here. It is not fine tuning of some of the changes that should be made, but take the whole darn thing, do away with it and bring in a system of real tax reform.
I want to cite some very specific problems which have been brought to my attention with respect to the application of the GST. I want to turn to a very specific situation such as the purchase of a new vehicle. Let me break it down into two arguments.
First I would like to look at a private citizen, a person who does not own or operate his own business, purchasing a vehicle. Then I would like to look at the situation of a business registrant purchasing a vehicle. This is someone who pays the GST, has a small business and uses a vehicle as part of that business. This is to show some of the specific problems that have not been addressed by this particular legislation.
First of all the private citizen who trades in his vehicle on a new one has to pay the full cost of the GST on the purchase of that new vehicle. That is fair enough if the consumer also recognizes that in fact there is essentially a tax credit being applied with the trade-in vehicle. That tax credit however goes to the dealer who purchases that vehicle.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
Here is where the problem lies. When that consumer trades in that vehicle he is bartering or negotiating on a fair trade-in value for the vehicle. He or she does not realize that what they are bargaining or bartering on in fact includes the 7 per cent GST. The car dealer will then get a GST credit for that when accounting for the sale of that vehicle on his books.
While the private citizen thinks he is getting 100 per cent of the value ol the vehicle the situation can be seen where the car dealer would negotiate the price of that vehicle down by 7 per cent to accommodate the cost of the GST, pick up the 7 per cent GST credit on the other side and basically walk away from the deal really without having paid anything in terms of the GST.
It is not the car dealer who has borne the brunt of the 7 per cent GST in that kind of situation. It is the purchaser of the new vehicle. The purchaser has paid the full price of the GST on the new vehicle and very likely may have unknowingly paid the 7 per cent GST on the trade-in value he received on that used vehicle.
I ask if that is fair. I really do not think it is. First of all, each individual dealer should be responsible for telling purchasers that the 7 per cent GST is rolled into that trade-in value and therefore they have to negotiate the cost of that trade-in based upon the 7 per cent that is applied. However, that is not happening so people are trading in vehicles not realizing they are essentially paying that trade-in cost.
The other situation is even more difficult. A business registrant purchases a new vehicle and has a vehicle which has been used at least 90 per cent of the time for business. That individual trades in that vehicle. The GST again is rolled into the trade-in value of that used vehicle and the car dealer who purchased that vehicle will of course be given the GST credit. What will happen is that the business registrant will pay the GST on the value of the new vehicle and on the value of the trade.
Here is where the real problem exists. I submit that probably 90 per cent of business owners who trade in a vehicle on a new one do not realize that they will be assessed through the business taxation for the trade-in of that vehicle. This is because as a business they are in fact selling that vehicle to the car dealer and they will be assessed. If the books are audited, you can be darn sure
that Revenue Canada will assess the 7 per cent GST on the trade-in of that vehicle. I want to restate that business owners are unaware that they could be audited and assessed the taxes on that vehicle.
That is a difficult situation because the car dealers are under no obligation to explain to the businessman or the individual citizen when they come in to purchase a new vehicle and trade in their old vehicle that the trade-in price actually includes the GST.
I want to read a letter from a chartered accountant in my home town of Vernon, British Columbia, which I think clearly lays out the argument. As I was mentioning, a business registrant negotiated the trade-in of a vehicle on a new vehicle and then was assessed the GST on the trade of that vehicle. He wrote: "The GST office states that unless a policy directive comes out from Ottawa they have no other choice of action and will not put in writing that the dealer is responsible to reimburse the registrant. They maintain that the only recourse open to the registrant is for him to take the matter to court".
Essentially he is saying that unless the purchaser of the new vehicle, the business owner, goes in and assesses the car dealer for the 7 per cent GST after the purchase goes through, there is no way of going back on it once he finds out. The car dealers are saying that the GST price is rolled into the negotiated trade-in value. Because they do not mention that to the customer, in this case the business customer, the customer has no way of knowing and after the fact has no way, other than through the courts, to reclaim the 7 per cent on the trade-in value due and owing to him.
To go back to the letter, Mr. Beardsell wrote: "This situation is unreasonable and could very easily be rectified by a change in assessing policy. Presently the dealer claims a notational credit of 7/107 on the trade-in received and the registrant is taxed by audit assessment on the trade-in. The government comes out even but the registrant is out of pocket by 7 per cent since the dealer is after the fact stating that the trade-in price includes the GST". He goes on to state: "If the auditor was simply instructed to assess the dealer instead of the registrant when he finds no GST is charged on the trade then fairness would be achieved".
March 12, 1993

The letter points out that a lot of business people are trading in their vehicles and paying the GST, not collecting it from the car dealer, not knowing that they have to, and later being hammered by Revenue Canada for the 7 per cent of the cost of their vehicles. That is simply unfair. It is also unfair that the government does not make clear in applying the GST toward the trade-in and the purchase of new vehicles that the onus is upon the purchaser of the vehicle, if he or she is a business person and uses the vehicle for business purposes, to collect the GST from the car dealer. It is terribly confusing. I am sure the people who will read my explanation of it will be as confused as members sitting here listening to my explanation of it. The whole process is terribly confusing.
With the confusion many people are being unnecessarily penalized by the 7 per cent GST on the trade-in of vehicles because they do not find out until well after the fact and there is no process for them other than through the courts.
This is only one aspect in which the GST has proven to be such a terrible headache. There are many other horror stories in terms of the application of this tax. But, for goodness sake, at least we could make things clear.
The government through its GST offices could clarify the point for the purchasers of vehicles. It could put the onus on car dealers to make sure that when people buy vehicles they know, if they are a private citizen, that the negotiated price of that trade-in includes the GST. They should also know that if they are a business registrant who is selling a vehicle to a car dealer to buy another vehicle from him they have to assess from the car dealer that 7 per cent GST on the cost of the trade-in vehicle they are selling the dealer. If they do not do so, come the end of the tax year they are going to be assessed through Revenue Canada.
How many business people know that? How many business people have been screwed on this? It is terribly unfair.
The government has to bring in some clarification. Tax accountants have been calling for them. I understand the car dealers lobbied to have it this way so that they could get away with this kind of stuff. I am not saying that every car dealer out there is surreptitiously using this little loophole to slide 7 per cent into their pockets. I am not saying they are all doing that, but I submit the option is
Government Orders
there should any unscrupulous dealer wish to do it. It has to be cleared up.
The government should instruct the car dealers through Revenue Canada that they have the responsibility to make this point very clear upon the sale of any vehicle. They have the moral responsibility and I would suggest the legal responsibility to make it clear.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Charest that Bill C-72, an act to establish the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Natural Resources envelope.

subtopic: NATIONAL ROUND TABLE ON THE ENVIRONMENT AND THE ECONOMY ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us today carries the title, an act to establish the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy.
In the limited time available I will focus on the weak side of this bill which as in many legislative measures also has positive and strong aspects. I will bring to the attention of the House what in my assessment is weak and requires modification.
Clause 4 of the bill outlines its purpose and subclauses (b) and (d) are not strong enough. Perhaps they are not clear enough. When defining the role of this round table to the effect that it advises the government on ways of incorporating environmental and economic considerations, the approach ought to be modified, re-examined and written in a different manner.

March 12, 1993
Government Orders
If we incorporate environmental and economic considerations we do not necessarily intend to mesh the two and integrate the two. Therefore we still treat the environment as a separate entity from the economy. It seems to me the purpose of this round table would be much better defined if it were instead to read under subclause (b): "advising governments on ways of meshing environmental and economic considerations". In so doing we will have said in different words what sustainable development is all about. That is the point I wanted to make.
In subclause (d) the round table should and is doing more than increasing public awareness. It is also promoting the understanding of sustainable development. That particular aspect of the role of the round table ought to be defined in subclause (d) of the purpose portion of the bill.
Finally, it seems to me that since the words sustainable development pop up on almost every page of this bill, particularly in the definitions section, setting the pace for the framework within which this bill is established and for the raison d'etre of the round table, actually the name of the round table ought to be changed and reflected in the title of the bill. Instead of the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy it ought to be renamed the national round table on sustainable development. That is what this round table is all about.
While this may seem to be semantics I would suggest it is more than that. What is being attempted here is to get across the importance of a concept that has emerged since the publication of the Brundtland report, Our Common Future, in 1987, namely the integration of the environment and the economy rather than their separation. We treat the environment and the economy as separate entities, but when we refer to a round table on sustainable development we automatically, by virtue of the use ol the term sustainable development, integrate the two. I hope I have succeeded in conveying the
importance of the concept of sustainable development and what it is all about.
In receiving this bill and debating it today there seems to be strange behaviour on the part of the government. Having axed the Economic Council of Canada, the Law Reform Commission, the Science Council of Canada and the Peace and Security Institute, we wonder why the government sees the necessity at this stage to give legislative status to the national round table. It almost makes us think of schizophrenic behaviour in a sense, having demolished on the one hand and on the other hand seeing the necessity to make up for its sins and giving the round table a legislative status. The round table can function with or without it, as we all know.
We are glad to support the initiative but we are puzzled when we ask ourselves how it fits into the over-all policy scheme of the government. This leads me to the third point I would like to make this afternoon.
I would like to compress my time so that my colleague from Edmonton Southeast can make an intervention before the adjournment. The basic question as we debate Bill C-72, an act to establish the National Round Thble on the Environment and the Economy, is how much of an impact the round table has had on government policies, on government decisions, since its inception.
The question must be put and not because the round table has been idle and unproductive. On the contrary, the round table has produced a wealth of documents, a wealth of intellectual input as already described in the debate yesterday by my colleagues. There is phenomenal enthusiasm and desire to advance the cause of sustainable development within a clear, cohesive and convincing intellectual framework.
What has been the impact on energy policy, on transportation policies, on agriculture, or most recently on overseas development? What has been the impact of the policy input that has been made available and which the government could have picked up on but by all evidence so far has not? Let me bring a couple of examples to your attention and then I will conclude.
March 12, 1993

First of all I will give you a minute example in the agricultural policies. I learned in March of last year of the decision of the Minister of Agriculture to exempt fertilizers from the GST. It does not make sense. Apart from the fact that the government lends itself to fierce criticism when people would understandably and quite rightly so inquire why exempt fertilizers but not books? What is so special about them?
As we stand here today in debate on this issue it has been a full 12 months since this harmless looking little regulation was announced by the Department of Agriculture in March 1992. Chemical pesticides are exempt from the GST. How do you reconcile it? It may have been only an anomaly, a strange behaviour on the part of the Minister of Agriculture under pressure. I do not know.
In last week's report by the National Transportation Act review commission we find another little item, recommendation No. 6 which reads: "We recommend that consideration of environmental methods not be addressed specifically in the National Transportation Act, but rather continue to fall under environmental protection statutes of general application". This is business as usual, the old outdated approach. It is not the approach the round table is desperately trying to advance on its agenda. In other words it does not make sense.
The mindset of those who have power does not take into account the changing times and the efforts being made by agencies and institutions such as the round table. Therefore the legitimacy of the question is whether it has an impact at the centre, whether it has an impact where it matters.
The most significant and disturbing example that one can raise in connection with this debate is the decision ol the Government of Canada to reduce its aid to developing countries and in particular to the less developed countries.
It does not make sense to learn as we did some 10 days ago that countries such as Niger, Ethiopia, Uganda, Mali and a number of Sahara region nations and others struggling desperately at the bottom of the human resources index produced by the UNDP will be cut by the Government of Canada in the name of debt reduction at home.
Government Orders
It does not make sense because if you look at the projects in which CIDA is engaged on behalf ol Canada in those countries, in those regions, you will see they are oriented to water, public health, agricultural rehabilitation and to fight desertification. All these are initiatives I am sure members opposite are very familiar with and actually which everybody in this House would want not to abandon, would want if anything to strengthen and expand.
One has to raise this issue in the context of this debate because it raises the question of the fight against poverty, on the issue of helping those who need help the most and within the broader concept of sustainable development which is the kind of development in which we believe at home as well as abroad. The round table has a big stake in the promotion of this agenda, in the movement toward these objectives. When you read that the Government of Canada decides to abolish, as in the case of Niger, a program that over five years amounts to some $12 million in water, in agriculture, in alternative sources of energy and in health, then you wonder what kind of contradictions we are facing and what on earth is going on.
My time is not quite up but I will be glad to share it with my colleague from Edmonton East. This is a very important issue and I thank you for your attention.

speechtext:
I would like to pick up the point of the question of cutting aid to countries like Niger and Uganda. I think it is one that all of us should be reflecting upon. Canada's aid has gone down from a peak of 0.5 per cent of GDP and could drop down to 0.3 per cent in the next three years.
It was pointed out this morning by The Globe and Mail, which is not always cited by those of us on this side of the House:
In 1974, when the debt was $25 billion, the federal government spent about one-tenth of its revenues on interest payments. In 1992, when the debt had soared to $425 billion, the proportion had risen to almost one-third.
Under pressure to stop the tide of debt, Ottawa is cutting $4.4 billion from its planned aid spending over five years. This may cause the cancellation of excellent programs such as the Canadian effort to rebuild the health system in Uganda. Unless something else happens and steps in to help health problems that are often lethal, impure water and poor hygiene will remain and people will die.
On the subject of Uganda I might point out to the members that the former High Commissioner of Canada to Uganda, who is a friend of mine, was working on AIDS research in a hospital in London, England when the new government asked him to come as their High Commissioner. He came for four years. He got aid re-established to Uganda. Now I understand that all of our aid to Uganda is going to be ended.
The question about a world in balance is one that is, I think, troubling to all thoughtful members in this House and one I think we all feel is a vital part of sustainable development around the world. The National Round Table on the Environment and Economy, as you know, has produced a series of excellent policy papers, for example, "On the Road to Brazil: The Earth Summit", "Trade, Environment and Competitiveness", "Discussion on Decision-Making Practices for Sustainable Development", "Sustainable Development: A Manager's Handbook", the "National waste reduction handbook", "Preserving Our World: a consumer's guide to the Brundtland Report" and "Toward Sustainable Communities: A resource book for municipal and local governments".
What Brundtland has said, as members know, is that sustainable development has to become a responsibility of all departments of government, probably most of all the Department of Finance which sent money off only recently for a project in the developing world which by any concept of sustainable development and human rights strikes me as at the least simply bizarre.
We have to get it into the heads of the people in the finance department, particularly the international section of the finance department, that they have to take greater account of sustainable development issues like population control around the world if we are to use Canadian tax dollars with some sense of stewardship. This is something that many Canadians feel is not now being done, particularly when the government is proposing to further reduce grants to the poorest nations in the world, quite contrary to CIDA's mandate, in favour of reallocating money to eastern Europe.
I am not saying that money should not go to eastern Europe, but for heaven's sake how can we spend $5.8 billion on submarine-chasing helicopters and yet turn and say to Uganda or Niger or many other nations in the developing world that we have no more money for them, but that we have money for the Rolls Royce of helicopters? It is something that I hope those on the other side will consider more and more. The public of Canada is firmly behind both opposition parties and I am sure members on the government side are saying this is the wrong expenditure at the wrong time and in the wrong way.
I have just a few thoughts, if I may, on the bill itself. I guess one is allowed to speak about the bill specifically when we are discussing a bill.

speechtext:
March 12, 1993
Private Members' Business
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider
the advisability of developing a healthy small business sector in
Canada by targeting more federal contracts to the small business
sector and establishing a more aggressive "Buy Canada" program.

Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure to support the motion of my friend and colleague, the member for Okanagan- Similkameen-Merritt.
This is a very important motion for small businesses right across Canada because it talks about the need to assist our small business community with an effective and aggressive buy Canada program.
I want to recite some statistical information relating to Canada's small business sector because I think a lot of people do not understand how important this particular sector is to the national economy. Certainly it is important to the economy throughout the Okanagan Valley which relies very heavily on tourism, the forestry sector and the agricultural sector, much of which employs our small business community.
Over 97 per cent of businesses throughout Canada are small businesses. Small businesses are defined as having under 50 employees. Looking at the figures from 1981 to 1989 over those years, small businesses created almost 82 per cent of the new jobs in Canada.
It is interesting to look at the number of jobs created by the small business sector compared to the number of jobs created over the same period of time in the large corporate sector, particularly the foreign-owned corporate sector. What we find is that with the foreign-owned interests in Canada there is actually a net job loss even though there is a substantial increase in net profits. There was a job loss from our large foreign-owned corporate sector whereas small businesses in Canada, taking the brunt of the responsibility, taking the brunt of the impact of the recession, were the ones still able to produce 82 per cent of the new jobs.
Almost 14,000 businesses declared bankruptcy in 1991 when the recession really started to take a bite. Business bankruptcies in the small business sector are up over 50 per cent since the recession began, with over 3,600 companies going under in the first three months of 1992 alone.
Small businesses are risky. They have difficulty in raising capital, in finding venture capital, in finding high-risk capital for acquisition and for expansion of the businesses. They have difficulty securing loans to maintain their businesses. The banking community is certainly
no friend of the small business community. They continually have to fight the high interest rate policy that this government has followed. Even though interest rates have come down somewhat over the past little while, our real interest rate, which is the difference between the interest rate and the inflationary rate, is still very much higher than it is in the United States. We still have a long way to go to bring that down to some degree of sensibility.
Another thing that has really hurt small business is the imposition of the GST. We know that the GST was introduced in large measure because the government was going to lose billions of dollars of revenue from the imposition of the tariff reductions under the FTA. In the first year alone over $2.2 billion was taken out of the revenues of the federal government as a result of the FTA. Who had to bear the burden of that? It was our consumers and our small business sector.
It needs some help. It is a vibrant sector of our economy, but it is a sector that is also the most vulnerable to the swings in our economy.
I would like to point out that the federal Department of Supply and Services purchases some $8 billion in goods and services on a competitive basis each year and some $3 billion on a non-competitive basis. These bids are solicited from lists of companies or individuals who have registered as potential suppliers. For low-dollar bids, less than $25,000 on a bid, Supply and Services Canada uses a rotational bidding system.
This bidding system requires that procurements be advertised to give businesses better access to government contracting opportunities. The Canadian sourcing policy limits competition for government procurement to domestic suppliers wherever possible. We also have some other programs in place, such as the Canadian content premium policy and the area buy policy, that have helped somewhat.
I want to point out a problem we have had since the free trade agreement was implemented, which has really put the concept of buying Canadian and helping our small business sector into jeopardy. According to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, Canada and the U.S. cannot protect domestic products or suppliers or discriminate against foreign products or suppliers who bid on purchases with a value of over $204,000. That is a pretty high value.
March 12, 1993

The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement dropped that threshold for competitive foreign bidding down to $29,000, which has had a very significant impact on our Canadian small business sector.
Let me point out that American federal departments and agencies are required to participate in a similar program in America. It is called the buy America program and favours suppliers based in the United States and gives preference to U.S. products. It is similar to Canada.
This act is also overruled somewhat by both the FTA and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, but there is a real difference between the limitations placed on Canadian small businesses and the limitations placed on small businesses in the U.S. Let me point out what the difference is.
In the United States the small business administration defines a small business as having up to 500 employees- that is considerably different than the definition in Canada-and up to $3.5 million in receipts. In Canada companies of this size are not considered small businesses. That is a fairly large corporation in Canada.
The U.S. small business act and small business set aside program are not affected by either GATT or the FTA, but the FTA prevents an effective buy Canada program. It affects the Canadian sourcing policy and the Canadian content policy for any purchases over $29,000. In the United States there is a similar situation but the dollar value is not anywhere near as low as Canada's.
Why is the United States allowed to effectively use protectionist trade practices that provide a much greater incentive to small businesses as they are defined in the United States than Canada is allowed to provide to small businesses as we define them in Canada? There is a substantial difference both in the definition and in the allowable limits.
Just to sum up very briefly, this points out one very particular way in which the provisions of the free trade agreement, as they are applied to the small business sector in Canada, have had such a dramatic impact in terms of allowing competitive foreign bids to come in for government procurement. This was one ol the reasons the government wanted to initiate the free trade agreement in the first place. It said that it would allow access to U.S. markets and U.S. government procurement. We see that the programs in the United States have protected its small business sector even under the provisions

of the free trade agreement much more so than we have in Canada.
What I am saying is that we have a situation where on the one hand small business in Canada is really under the gun as a result of the free trade agreement. On the other hand, small business in the United States has been given much more latitude and much more protection.
As a result of that, my colleague the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt has brought in this private member's motion to try and convince this government of the error of its ways. It is hoped this will convince the government that we need some action to help our small business communities, our entrepreneurs from Victoria to St. John's. We need to help them not with a hand-out but with a hand-up. Give them a boost so we can put people back to work in Canada and help our small business community once again become the vibrant job-creating engine it has been in the past.

speechtext: Debate, the hon. member for Red Deer. The hon. member has two minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think that I will need two minutes. The hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt asked me for an indication as to whether or not I was going to support his motion. He knows very well that I have relatives who live in his riding. Unfortunately one of them voted for him which shows a little bad judgment on her part.
I do think this member has shown a little bit of good judgment in this motion and I have no trouble at all in supporting it. The principle in it is real. The government should be supporting small business because, as the previous speaker indicated, small business is the heart of our economy. It is what makes this country go.
While I have the floor I also want to indicate that the Chamber of Commerce in my riding of Red Deer has connected into a computerized program of electronic bulletin boards. It is making information available to its members. Its members in Red Deer have had access to three times as many government contracts during the past year as they have had in the past two years. It is working. The contracts are available to small business.
I am not sure what the hon. member is intending with this motion but it is certainly not going to hurt us to discuss it a little further and to encourage it. It is a good objective and I definitely support it and will be indicating so later.
